cards.explanation: The answer is a lawyer named Tertullus. Ananias, the high priest, came down with some elders and a lawyer named Tertullus. Tertullus is the one who presented their case against Paul to the governor. A lawyer doing the talking makes sense to me, friends, like the person at the counter who actually knows how to fill out the form.

The answer is that Felix brought the nation lasting peace. Tertullus says, “Because of you, we have enjoyed a lasting peace, and your foresight has brought improvements to this nation.” He's talking about the judge before he says a word about the prisoner. I think it sounds like a five-star review from somebody who's about to ask for a refund.

The answer is a ringleader. Tertullus calls Paul “…a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes…” That means the one out front, the one everybody is supposedly following. It's a big claim to make about a man standing there under guard, friends.
The word is seized. Tertullus says Paul even tried to desecrate the temple, “so we seized him.” That's the accusers' side of the story, bakers. Paul is about to give his own.
The answer is True. Verse 9 says the Jews concurred, asserting that these charges were true. So Tertullus isn't speaking alone. The people with him join in and say the charges are true.

The word is gladly! Paul says, “Knowing that you have been a judge over this nation for many years, I gladly make my defense.” He's standing in front of a governor with the high priest and a lawyer against him, and he says gladly. Friends, I'd have been sweating through my apron.

The word is worship. Paul says it was no more than twelve days ago that he went up to Jerusalem to worship. He tells Felix he can verify it for himself. I bet he's glad the dates can be checked, friends.

The answer is False. Paul says his accusers did not find him debating with anyone in the temple or riling up a crowd in the synagogues or in the city. He's answering Tertullus point by point, bakers. And he adds that they can't prove any of their charges.

The answer is that he worships God according to the Way. Paul says, “I do confess to you, however, that I worship the God of our fathers according to the Way, which they call a sect.” It isn't a crime he's confessing. It's the center of his life. I think that's a pretty bold thing to admit with the accusers sitting right there.

The answer is that the righteous and the wicked will rise again. Paul says he has the same hope in God that his accusers cherish, “…that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked.” Both groups, friends, not just one. That's a hope he says he shares with the very men accusing him.

The answer is to bring alms and present offerings. That's what Paul says. After several years, he returned to Jerusalem “…to bring alms to my people and to present offerings.” That's the reason he gives Felix for the trip, friends.

The answer is True. Paul says, “At the time they found me in the temple, I was ceremonially clean and was not inciting a crowd or an uproar.” He's answering the charge that he tried to desecrate the temple (Acts 24:6). Clean, calm and no uproar is how he describes himself that day, bakers.

The answer is False. Paul says the one thing he called out before the Sanhedrin was, “It is concerning the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you today.” Nothing in his words there mentions the Law of Moses, friends. The thing he names is the resurrection.

The word is friends. Felix orders the centurion to keep Paul under guard, but to allow him some freedom and permit his friends to minister to his needs. So Paul is under guard, and his friends are still allowed to help him. I'd take that over the back of the junk drawer I spent years stuck in.

The word is frightened. As Paul expounded on righteousness, self-control and the coming judgment, Felix became frightened. Paul wasn't just reading out a to-do list, friends. Whatever else was going on in that room, Felix heard it and it shook him.

The answer is a bribe. The text says Felix was hoping Paul would offer him a bribe, so he sent for Paul frequently and talked with him. I think that explains why the visits kept coming. It's still a hard thing to read, friends, about a man who just heard about righteousness.

The answer is that he leaves Paul in prison. The text says, “…wishing to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.” Two years had passed and Festus was taking over, and Paul was still sitting there. I think this is a heavy part of the story, friends, and it's good that the story isn't over.
